title: Jacobson's perfect attack and Thomas's teaching ambitions
summary: He calls Jacobson a genius, describes the tongue-on-reed attack, and says he wanted to teach only after studying with him; a Kansas professor is mentioned.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Reeds, mouthpieces and horns: the reed player's gear

blocks.x: He was in ....(?).... space in Boston, across from Symphony Hall. It was upstairs on the sixth floor, wasn't it.
Yeah, I think so.
I can remember, I went up there with you. Because I remember waiting in the waiting room.
Boy, he was a genius.
So now, we're...

And the beautiful thing about him, he had a radio show every day. So you could listen to him and hear him play. And he played alto, boy...and clarinet... Oh, he had the most beautiful clarinet. But that subtone... And I was so glad to study with him. Because see, I had always had aspirations to teach. I don't know why. But after I'd learned how to play saxophone pretty good, I wanted to teach. And I was so glad I didn't start teaching until after I studied with him.

Because he actually showed me the secret of playing the saxophone. See, his way of doing it was that once you attack, let the tongue be all the way down in the mouth and in front of your mouth, touching your lip, and the teeth is in front. That way it's relaxed. But if you draw your tongue back, like most guys are taught, you're closing your
Thomas - 88

throat up. And he just said, "You know what's the most perfect attack?" Now, this is what startled me. He said, "The most perfect attack is put your tongue on the reed, and as you blow, take it off." Because that starts...the tongue starts there. That's the perfect attack. Put your tongue on the reed, and as you blow, take it off. Just ...[RELAXED EXHALATION] The note comes out. I've had so many guys come to me and study with me, and they had problems, and I could tell them in a minute, because... The average guy thinks that a saxophone is hard to play. There ain't nothin' to it.
There's a teacher out in Kansas, a professor at one of the universities who studied with you...
Yeah, I met him.
He used to speak all the time about you.
Yeah, I met him. He's around Wichita or something.
Yeah, Wichita.
I met him. He came to New York, and I had a session with him.
Yes. He was a Doctor of Philosophy or something...
Yes, one of them...it starts with an "A".
Anthropology.
Thomas - 89
Yes, anthropology...
Why don't we just get back to the bands...
